vignette:
The Weight of Smoke and Spice

Rajan is a 44-year-old South Asian man who works as a head chef at a mid-sized restaurant in a city far from the country where he was born. He has lived in this place for nearly eleven years now, long enough to have built something that resembles a life, though he would be the first to tell you, in his careful, measured way, that the life he has now is not the one he was supposed to have.

He left his home country in his early thirties, not by choice but by necessity. The political violence that swept through his region had been building for years, but it arrived at his family's door with sudden, terrible speed. He witnessed the burning of his neighborhood, the disappearance of two cousins whose names he still cannot say aloud, and endured weeks of displacement through transit camps where safety was never guaranteed and dignity was rarely offered. The journey that eventually brought him here took almost two years, moving through countries that did not want him, sleeping in places he tries not to remember. He arrived with a single bag, a culinary training certificate that almost wasn't accepted, and a silence around him so thick it took his first employer months to realize how capable he actually was.

In the kitchen, Rajan is precise and controlled. His coworkers describe him as excellent but difficult to know. He arrives early, leaves late, and fills the hours between with a focused intensity that his sous chef admires but also finds slightly unnerving. What his coworkers don't see is that the kitchen is the one place where the noise in his head becomes manageable. The heat, the movement, the demands of service - they occupy just enough of his attention to keep certain images from surfacing. He has organized his life, without quite meaning to, around the principle of staying busy enough not to feel.

Outside of work, things are harder. He lives alone in a small apartment he keeps meticulously clean. He does not sleep well. Most nights he wakes between two and four in the morning, heart already racing before he is fully conscious, the specific smell of burning from those weeks of displacement somehow present in a room where nothing is burning at all. He lies still and waits for it to pass, which it does, eventually, though it always takes longer than he thinks it should.

He does not watch the news. He deleted social media several years ago after a video appeared in his feed - unrelated to his own experience, just a news clip - and he found himself unable to move from his chair for nearly an hour. He has not explained this to anyone. He has not explained most things to anyone. His relationships tend to be cordial and shallow, not because he dislikes people but because closeness requires a kind of disclosure he cannot yet manage. He has been single for six years. He tells himself this suits him.

What brings him in now is something small, which is often how it goes. A new line cook joined the restaurant last month, a young man who reminds Rajan of one of his disappeared cousins - the same way of laughing, the same habit of tucking a towel into his apron strings. Rajan finds himself watching this young man with a grief so sudden and physical that he has had to step into the walk-in cooler twice to compose himself. He has started leaving work earlier than usual. He is sleeping even less.

He sits across from the therapist with his hands folded in his lap, speaking quietly and precisely, the same way he plates a dish - with great care, and with the sense that something fragile is being handled. He says he is fine, mostly. He says he just wanted to talk to someone. Then he pauses for a long moment and says that he thinks about his cousins every single day, and that he has never told anyone that before.
